role.title: OT Cybersecurity Engineer (Manufacturing)
role.description: DRAFT. A manufacturing specialization of NICE work role DD-WRL-009 (Operational Technology (OT) Cybersecurity Engineering). Engineers the security of manufacturing control systems (PLC-based production lines and machine cells, and the operations systems that schedule and track them) so that plants keep producing safely and to specification despite intentional or accidental cyber events. Works with controls engineers, machine builders and integrators, plant operations and maintenance, and IT security.

citations.note: Request process for remote access, temporary vendor access, removal when no longer required (timers), monitoring remote activity, labeling devices for quick disconnection.

statements.text: Define controls for transient cyber assets and removable media brought into production areas

citations.note: Restricts removable media and devices on OT nodes; does not use the term transient cyber assets.

statements.text: Schedule cybersecurity changes (e.g., patches, firmware updates, firewall rule changes) around production schedules and planned downtime, with tested rollback

citations.note: Schedule changes in maintenance downtime to limit impact.
Test patches in a test environment first.

statements.text: Assess the security of engineering workstations and controller programming software

citations.note: RBAC on engineering workstations.

statements.text: Map ATT&CK for ICS techniques to the plant's assets and processes to prioritize mitigations

citations.locator: §4.1.2 Assessing Risk in an OT Environment (PDF p. 68)
citations.note: Refers to ATT&CK for ICS in risk assessment.

statements.text: Specify network monitoring requirements for passive visibility of industrial protocol traffic within and between plant zones
Specify cybersecurity requirements in machine-builder and integrator contracts for new production equipment

citations.locator: Appendix F.7.16 System and Services Acquisition (PDF pp. 297-298)
citations.note: Contracts with third-party integrators.

statements.text: Identify the critical functions where cyber manipulation could cause unacceptable consequences, and focus security design effort on them first
Specify engineered controls early in design that eliminate or limit high-consequence cyber-enabled outcomes, instead of relying only on added IT security controls
Design information pathways so that data flows only in intended directions, and enforce those flows with architectural controls

citations.locator: Principles of CIE: Secure information architecture (p. 13)

statements.text: Limit digital functionality to what each function needs, removing high-consequence, low-value complexity and latent capabilities that attackers could misuse
Design layered defenses with diversity, redundancy and hardening so that a single failure cannot disable a critical function and degradation during an incident is predictable

citations.locator: Principles of CIE: Resilient layered defenses (p. 13)

statements.text: Include design elements that detect intrusions and allow a threat to be isolated or removed while critical operations continue
Evaluate, with safety, quality, maintenance and other disciplines, how misuse of a digital system could affect their areas of operation
Plan for continued operation during and after a cyber attack that degrades digital controls, assuming any digital component may be compromised during its lifecycle

citations.locator: Principles of CIE: Planned resilience with no assumed security (p. 14)

statements.text: Protect sensitive engineering records (e.g., requirements, specifications, designs, configurations, test results) whose release would help attackers

citations.locator: Principles of CIE: Engineering information control (p. 14)

statements.text: Knowledge of the ISA-95 (IEC 62264) functional hierarchy and how manufacturing operations systems (e.g., MES, batch and recipe management) map onto Purdue levels and network zones

citations.note: Names Purdue model and ISA-95 levels as reference architectures for segmentation.
Defines the ISA-95 functional hierarchy; cited by part only.

statements.text: Knowledge of industrial protocol families common in manufacturing (e.g., EtherNet/IP and CIP, PROFINET, Modbus TCP, OPC UA) and which security features each does or does not provide

citations.note: Discusses OT protocols and their security limitations; exact section not yet pinned.
Command messages sent over industrial protocols without authentication.

statements.text: Knowledge of controller programs and engineering project files (e.g., IEC 61131-3 ladder diagram, structured text, function block diagram) as security-critical assets

citations.note: Treats PLC logic and configuration files as data to back up and protect.
Defines the controller programming languages; cited by part only.

statements.text: Knowledge of controller operating modes and mode protection (e.g., physical key switches, run, program and remote modes) and how mode changes enable logic or firmware changes

citations.locator: Appendix F.7.5 Configuration Management, CM-3 control enhancement (8) OT discussion (PDF p. 261)
citations.note: Describes PLC key switches used to restrict program changes.

statements.text: Knowledge of vendor, machine-builder and integrator access paths into manufacturing networks (e.g., remote support connections, remote access built into machines, on-site service laptops)

citations.note: Covers temporary vendor remote access and its controls.
Security requirements for IACS service providers (integrators, maintenance).

statements.text: Knowledge of how cyber events in manufacturing become production consequences such as line stoppage, scrap, latent quality defects and equipment damage

citations.note: Lists Maintain Production Goals and Maintain Quality of Product among manufacturing business/mission objectives.
Notes extended downtimes and production losses.

statements.text: Knowledge of Cyber-Informed Engineering (CIE) principles and consequence-driven analysis methods

citations.note: Defines the 12 CIE principles in design/operational and organizational groups.

citations.locator: Appendix D.2.7 INL CIE and CCE (PDF p. 215)

statements.text: Knowledge of MITRE ATT&CK for ICS tactics and techniques

citations.locator: Appendix D.3.5 MITRE ATT&CK for ICS (PDF p. 218)

statements.text: Knowledge of engineered controls that limit physical consequences independently of digital control systems (e.g., mechanical interlocks, relief devices, hardwired trips, physical travel limits)
Knowledge of the systems engineering lifecycle (concept through retirement) and the cybersecurity choices available to engineers in each phase

citations.locator: Part A, Systems Engineering Lifecycle Model for CIE (p. 10)
Key Premises of the National CIE Strategy (p. 15)
citations.note: Risk can be reduced across the lifecycle, most cheaply early in design.

statements.text: Skill in reading controller logic (e.g., ladder diagram, structured text, function block diagram) to find security-relevant behavior such as hidden overrides or altered setpoints

citations.locator: Appendix C.3 Threat Events and Incidents (PDF p. 196)

statements.text: Skill in configuring controller and engineering-software security features (e.g., access passwords, mode protection, protected program blocks)

citations.locator: Appendix F.7.5 Configuration Management, CM-3 control enhancement (8) OT discussion (PDF p. 261)

statements.text: Skill in analyzing industrial protocol traffic to tell normal process communication from unauthorized commands

citations.note: A baseline of normal OT traffic helps separate attacks from transient conditions.

statements.text: Skill in testing OT security controls without disrupting production (e.g., passive methods first, test environments, coordination with operations)

citations.note: Active scans can affect device process state.

statements.text: Skill in tracing how manipulation of a digital function could lead to a physical consequence

modules.objective: Identify unauthorized setpoint modifications in Structured Text.
Execute containment and recovery steps with process continuity and safety constraints.
Execute recovery steps and verify logic integrity after a controller reflash.
Identify MBAP header length anomalies in Modbus TCP traffic
Recognize a ENIP command and its direct physical consequence.
Analyze CIP service codes to detect unauthorized controller state manipulation.
Analyze ladder logic to detect unauthorized changes.
Reconstruct an adversary timeline to identify unauthorized control nodes and tampered ENIP/CIP setpoints.
Detect unauthorized logic changes in Structured Text.
Identify the missing field in a truncated (Partial) MBAP header.
Reconstruct adversary timeline using historian and network layers.
Execute containment steps while maintaining process stability.
Communicate risk to leadership regarding network architecture.
Perform packet analysis to extract a setpoint modification.
Perform packet analysis to reconstruct a multi-state control change.
Interpret control logic and correlate behavior to a physical process.
Compare baseline vs modified logic state for hidden manipulation.
Identify a hidden logic override in a ladder logic comparison.
